messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Mariana arrived for her first session at forty minutes to seven, just after the community center where she worked had closed for the evening. She was thirty-eight, a community organizer in a midsize city, and she chose the chair in the corner of the office before the therapist could offer one—a habit so automatic she did not seem to notice she had done it. She sat with her back against the wall, her eyes moving across the room in a slow, practiced sweep, and then she folded her hands in her lap and began to speak.

The event she carried with her had happened when she was nine years old, in the apartment of her mother’s then-boyfriend, a man named Eduardo who had been living with them for about a year. What Mariana remembered was not a continuous story but a series of images, some of them so sharp they felt like photographs held too close to her face, and others that were simply gone. She remembered the way the linoleum in the kitchen felt against her cheek, the pattern of small brown diamonds repeating under her eye. She remembered the weight of Eduardo’s hand on the back of her neck, pressing her face down. She did not remember how she had gotten to the kitchen floor, or how she had gotten up afterward, or whether she had cried. There were hours of that afternoon that were simply blank, and she had never been able to fill them in. Sometimes, when she tried to recall what had happened, she felt nothing at all—a kind of deadness spreading through her chest, as though the memory belonged to someone else, a girl she did not know and could not quite feel sorry for.

For a long time after that year, Mariana had told herself that the past was the past and that she was fine. She finished high school, put herself through community college, and found her way into organizing work—first with a tenants’ rights group, then with a coalition fighting displacement in the neighborhood where she had grown up. She was good at her job. She was known for being relentless, for staying late, for taking on more than anyone else on the team. She threw herself into campaigns the way other people threw themselves into relationships: completely, until there was nothing left over. It was how she kept her mind from drifting into the images she did not want to see. As long as she was in a meeting, or writing a press release, or knocking on doors, she did not have to deal with the sudden arrival of that kitchen floor in her mind, the brown diamonds, the pressure of a hand.

But the work could not fill everything. At night, when she tried to fall asleep, her body refused to let go. She lay in bed with her eyes open, listening to the sounds of the house, her muscles tensed as if she needed to be ready for something. Her partner, Daniel, had learned to sleep on his side facing away from her, because if he moved too quickly or too close she would startle and be awake for another hour. She had never told him why. She had never told anyone the full story, because she was certain that if she had been stronger—if she had been a different kind of person—she would have stopped it. Somebody else would have known what to do. Somebody else would have pushed him away, or run, or told someone afterward. But she had not done any of those things, and that fact had become the story she told herself about who she was: a weak person, someone who could not protect herself, someone who had not even tried.

In daily life, this belief translated into a constant, low-level vigilance. She checked behind her when she walked to her car. She scanned every room before she entered it, looking for exits, looking for corners, looking for the seat that would let her see the door and the windows at once. If a restaurant or a coffee shop had only tables in the middle of the floor, she would leave rather than sit exposed. She had stopped going to crowded events unless she could arrive early and claim a spot against a wall. At work, her colleagues had learned not to sit behind her in meetings; she had snapped at someone once, without explanation, and now they simply gave her the corner seat by unspoken agreement.

What finally brought Mariana to therapy was not the hypervigilance or the overwork or the sleeplessness. It was a moment during a coalition meeting the previous month. She had been standing at the front of the room, presenting a proposal, when a memory surfaced without warning—the linoleum, the pressure, the smell of Eduardo’s cologne—and for a few seconds she lost her place in the sentence. She had recovered quickly, or so she thought, but afterward she sat in her car and tried to make the images stop. She tried to erase them, to push them back down into the blank spaces where they belonged, but they would not go. She had come to understand, in that moment, that she could not keep working hard enough to outrun what she was carrying. She was afraid of what would happen if she stopped. She was afraid of what she might find if she let herself feel it. But she was also, for the first time in a long time, exhausted. And so she had called.
